question:
Patient note:
A 55-year-old man presented to the acute assessment area late this morning complaining that his right lower leg had looked “pumped up like a football” since waking yesterday and had become progressively sore when he tried to stand. Six days earlier he developed a febrile influenza-like illness that left him exhausted and febrile to 38.7 °C; fearing he might pass the virus to his elderly parents, he isolated himself in a spare bedroom where, by his own estimate taken from the step counter on his phone, he averaged fewer than 400 steps per day and spent roughly twenty-two hours each day supine between Monday evening and Friday afternoon. He noted only brief bathroom trips and occasional shuffles to the kitchen for fluids, and he did not resume normal mobility until the fever abated late Friday night. Saturday was the first time he walked around the house for a full hour, and on Sunday morning he noticed that the lower half of the right leg felt tight inside his pajama bottoms while the rest of the limb appeared unchanged. The discomfort has remained localised to the calf region, without radiating into the thigh, knee, ankle, or foot, and he denies redness, streaking, skin breakdown, insect bites, blunt trauma, or vigorous exercise preceding onset. He also denies chest pain, dyspnoea, cough, palpitations, haemoptysis, syncope, flank pain, dysuria, or abdominal discomfort. There is no prior history of clots in the legs or lungs, no known thrombophilia, and he has never been prescribed anticoagulants. Past medical history includes well-controlled primary hypertension managed with losartan 100 mg daily and dyspepsia treated with omeprazole 20 mg nightly; he has no malignancies, heart failure, inflammatory bowel disease, chronic kidney disease, or recent hospitalisations. The patient underwent an uncomplicated laparoscopic appendicectomy nine years ago but has had no operative procedures, endoscopies, or catheter placements in the last twelve months. He does not smoke, consumes one or two beers on weekends, and denies illicit drug use. Family history is unremarkable for venous or arterial thromboembolic disease. On arrival—prior to any analgesic, intravenous fluid, or antithrombotic therapy—he was seated with the right leg elevated on a pillow. Vital signs were temperature 36.8 °C, blood pressure 142/84 mm Hg, heart rate 92 beats per minute and regular, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 97 % breathing ambient air. He appeared mildly uncomfortable but conversed coherently. Cardiovascular examination revealed a brisk carotid upstroke and distinct S1 and S2 with no murmurs, rubs, or gallops; lungs were clear to auscultation. The abdomen was soft and non-tender with no organomegaly. Inspection of the lower extremities disclosed visible asymmetry confined to the calf segment: a flexible tape positioned exactly 10 cm below the tibial tuberosity measured 44.0 cm in circumference on the right and 39.6 cm on the left, giving a difference of 4.4 cm; mid-thigh girths were 55.2 cm bilaterally, and ankle circumferences differed by less than 0.5 cm. Skin over both legs was warm and uniformly pink without hyperpigmentation, ulceration, or engorged subcutaneous channels, and hair distribution was equal. Gentle thumb pressure over the pre-tibial surface was unrevealing; the examiner chose not to repeat deeper indentation to avoid unnecessary discomfort. Palpation with two fingers tracing the expected course of the femoral vein just distal to the inguinal ligament, through the adductor canal, behind the knee, and into the proximal posterior calf provoked a sharply localised ache most pronounced at the popliteal fossa and along the medial gastrocnemius belly, whereas comparable pressure over the quadriceps and anterior tibial compartment elicited only diffuse blunt pressure. No palpable cord, fluctuance, or crepitus was detected. Hip, knee, and ankle ranges of motion were full, though plantarflexion against resistance intensified the deep soreness. Distal pulses—dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial—were 2 + and symmetric; capillary refill at the toes was <2 s, and light-touch sensation was intact throughout. There was no neurological weakness and no casts, splints, or braces on either limb. Inguinal lymph nodes were not enlarged. A point-of-care complete blood count drawn before any therapy showed haemoglobin 14.1 g/dL, white blood cell count 7.4 × 10⁹/L, and platelets 238 × 10⁹/L; basic metabolic profile revealed serum creatinine 0.93 mg/dL, sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 4.3 mmol/L, and bicarbonate 24 mmol/L. International normalised ratio was 1.0 and activated partial thromboplastin time 29 s. A 12-lead electrocardiogram demonstrated normal sinus rhythm at 90 beats per minute with no ST-T abnormalities, and a portable anteroposterior chest radiograph showed clear lung fields. No musculoskeletal tear, cellulitis, ruptured Baker cyst, or venous varicosity could be identified to plausibly account for the unilateral calf enlargement and discrete deep-tract tenderness in the context of the recent prolonged recumbency, so urgent duplex imaging of the right lower extremity venous system was requested while the patient remained hemodynamically stable in the observation bay.

Question: What is the patient's score of Wells' criteria for Deep Vein Thrombosis? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Wells DVT score assigns 1 point per positive clinical criterion and subtracts 2 if an alternative diagnosis is at least as likely as DVT. At presentation:
- Recent bed rest for at least 3 days or qualifying recent surgery: nearly continuously supine from Monday evening to Friday afternoon, with only brief trips out of bed → +1.
- Localized tenderness along the deep venous system: present in the popliteal fossa and proximal calf → +1.
- Calf circumference at least 3 cm greater on the symptomatic side, measured 10 cm below the tibial tuberosity: 44.0 − 39.6 = 4.4 cm → +1.
- Active cancer, lower-limb paralysis/paresis or cast immobilization, whole-leg swelling, unilateral pitting edema, nonvaricose collateral superficial veins, and prior DVT: none documented → 0 each.
- No alternative diagnosis was judged at least as likely → no deduction.
Total = 1 + 1 + 1 = 3.
Final answer: 3
